title: The rooster crows (Luke 22:54–62)
hook: Peter swears three times he never knew him, then the rooster, then the look

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gethsemane: take this cup, and then, not my will. That same night, soldiers come to the garden.

Pretending not to know someone. Laughing along. Keeping quiet when you meant to speak. It can happen in a second, before anyone has decided anything. A courtyard in Jerusalem, in the middle of the night. Jesus has been arrested and taken into the high priest's house. Mark says the others fled. But Peter, who walked on water, who said he'd go to prison and to death with him, follows at a distance. He slips into the courtyard and sits down by a fire with the servants and guards, warming his hands.
screen: `PRETENDING NOT TO KNOW SOMEONE.` → `ARRESTED IN THE NIGHT.` → `PETER BY THE FIRE.`

segments.voice: A servant girl looks at him in the firelight and says: this man was with him. And Peter, in the King James Bible: "Woman, I know him not." A little later someone else: you're one of them. "Man, I am not." About an hour later, a third person insists: surely this fellow was with him, for he's a Galilean. And Peter says: "Man, I know not what thou sayest." While he's still speaking, the rooster crows. Earlier that evening Jesus had told him exactly this, and Peter had said never. Then Luke adds a detail no other Gospel has: "And the Lord turned, and looked upon Peter." Across the courtyard, their eyes meet. Luke doesn't describe the look. Angry? Sad? Loving? The sources are silent. "And Peter remembered the word of the Lord, how he had said unto him, Before the cock crow, thou shalt deny me thrice. And Peter went out, and wept bitterly." This story is in all four Gospels. The first Christians could have left out the night Peter failed; all four kept it. Peter, the rock, the one with the keys, is also the one who said three times, I don't know him. And failure isn't where his story ends. Tradition links the rooster on top of some church steeples to this night: a reminder to stay awake, and that even Peter fell, and was not finished.
screen: `WOMAN, I KNOW HIM NOT.` · `THREE TIMES, THEN THE ROOSTER.` · `THE LORD TURNED AND LOOKED.` · `TOLD IN ALL FOUR GOSPELS.` · then, large: `PETER WENT OUT, AND WEPT BITTERLY.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one old failure you still carry, a time you let someone down, or yourself, and look at it once, honestly, without replaying it; notice how long you've been carrying it. Think of Peter weeping in the dark, whose story didn't end there, and say to yourself quietly: that happened, and I'm more than that. If you pray, you can ask to be forgiven and to forgive yourself.
Cock crow. The King James phrase for the sound that stopped Peter mid-denial, the third time, exactly when Jesus had said it would.
Your line: even Peter. His story didn't end by the fire. Day sixty-seven, done.

howItsDone: Peter's denial is read in Holy Week in many churches, and it's sung in the Passion settings of Bach and others. Weathervanes shaped like roosters sit on some church steeples, especially in Europe.

original.note: Greek: a rooster. The bird that crowed after Peter's third denial.

what a scholar hears: all four Gospels keep this embarrassing story about Peter, and only Luke has the look across the courtyard.

chat.says: Why would the Gospels tell about Peter denying Jesus? Isn't that embarrassing?
options: All four kept it: even Peter failed, and failure wasn't where his story ended.
It shows that Peter was never really a true disciple to begin with.
They kept it as a warning that a failure like that can't be forgiven.
chat.meaning: The first Christians could have left out the night Peter failed; all four Gospels kept it. Even Peter fell, and was not finished.

cock crow.meaning: the rooster's crowing, the sound that stopped Peter mid-denial

Galilean.meaning: someone from Galilee, in the north, like Peter

high priest.meaning: the head of the temple's priests; Jesus was taken to his house

notes: 'In all four Gospels' (Matthew 26:69–75; Mark 14:66–72; Luke 22:54–62; John 18:15–27). The look (22:61) is unique to Luke.
The rooster on church steeples as a symbol linked to Peter; commonly stated (a ninth-century papal decree is often cited). Confirm.
Bach's St Matthew and St John Passions include the denial ('Erbarme dich' follows it in the St Matthew). Confirm howItsDone.
The practice invites self-forgiveness and does not tell the listener what to believe; 'if you pray' framing.
Carry is lowercase 'even peter' in the index; kept exactly.
